news_title: Salmonella sickens 60 at hospital in Costa Rica - Food Safety News
efet_title: Salmonella sickens 60 at hospital in Costa Rica - Food Safety News
efet_body:
More than 60 people have fallen sick in Costa Rica as part of a Salmonella outbreak connected to a hospital. The U.S. Embassy in Costa Rica has issued an alert.
Costa Rica’s Ministry of Health (MOH) reported an outbreak of Salmonella at Hospital CIMA in Escazú.
In total, 66 cases have been recorded, two have been confirmed by laboratory testing, and two patients have been hospitalized. Lab analysis identified Salmonella in confirmed cases.
Reported symptoms include diarrhea, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, fever, and general malaise, according to the alert from the U.S. Embassy in Costa Rica.
The Ministry of Health is trying to identify any common exposures in those affected and the mode of transmission. Reports describe illness among hospital workers. No specific food has been identified, and the source of contamination has not been confirmed.
The U.S. Embassy advised its personnel to consider alternative locations for medical care until the outbreak has been resolved.
Other advice is to practice consistent hand hygiene with soap and water, especially after using the restroom and before preparing or eating food.
Keep raw and cooked foods separate, cook eggs, poultry, and meat thoroughly, and refrigerate perishable foods promptly. Wash fruits and vegetables before consumption and avoid unpasteurized dairy products. People with gastrointestinal illness should not prepare food for others while symptomatic.
Mexican outbreak
In early September, another Salmonella outbreak occurred at a hospital in Mexico.
Health officials confirmed that 135 people fell sick at the Hospital General de México Dr. Eduardo Liceaga.
The outbreak was linked to food provided by the hospital’s outsourced catering service. Patients experienced symptoms such as abdominal pain, diarrhea, fever, and vomiting.
In two cases, a coinfection with enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC) was also identified.
The hospital suspended the outsourced dining service and opened an investigation to identify and monitor individuals who may have been exposed.
An epidemiological and health investigation was started to determine the source of contamination and to establish additional prevention and control measures.

news_title: E. coli infections reported among children who visited pumpkin patches, petting zoos - Food Safety News
efet_title: E. coli infections reported among children who visited pumpkin patches, petting zoos - Food Safety News
efet_body:
The County of San Luis Obispo, CA, Department of Public Health has confirmed five cases of Shiga toxin-producing E. coli infection and is investigating a potential link to Brookshire Farms in San Luis Obispo. The suspected exposure period is Oct. 16 through 26. The source of the infections is under investigation.
Anyone who visited Brookshire Farms pumpkin patch or corn maze between Oct. 16 and 26 and is experiencing gastrointestinal symptoms, usually cramping abdominal pain and bloody diarrhea, typically 3-10 days after their visit should contact their healthcare provider. Children under the age of 10 are at highest risk of having complications. Individuals contacted by Public Health investigators are strongly encouraged to cooperate with requests for information to help identify the source of the infections.
“We are working diligently to identify the source of these infections to protect the health of our community,” said County Health Officer Dr. Christy Mulkerin. “We encourage anyone who may have been exposed and is experiencing symptoms consistent with E. coli infection to seek immediate medical attention.”
Brookshire Farms has closed while Public Health completes its investigation and whether additional community members may be at risk. Public Health is also gathering information, investigating potential exposures and conducting follow-up activities to determine whether the cases are connected.
According to the farm’s promotional listings, in addition to the pumpkin patch, it offers hayrides, grain-cart rides, pedal carts, a jumping pillow, duck races, a playground, a hay climb, a hay maze and a corn maze, and
a U-pick directory lists
farm animals.
Meanwhile, investigations continue at Bengtson’s Pumpkin Farm in Homer Glen, IL, where four of five children with E. coli infections have been hospitalized. All five visited the farm before becoming ill.
Bengtson’s closed its petting zoo on Oct. 23 and kept the rides, food stands and corn maze open. Animal and environmental samples were taken on Oct. 26, results are expected around Nov.5.
If your child visited Brookshire Farms between Oct. 16 and 26, or Bengtson’s on or after Sept. 29, and develops bloody diarrhea, severe cramps, decreased urination, unusual paleness or lethargy, see a doctor and tell them about the farm visit. HUS can develop a week or more after the diarrhea starts.

Joe explains how investigators are tracing suspected sources, why some outbreaks persist for years, and how gaps in international data sharing complicate the response. Morgan and Jonan also break down the week’s food safety headlines, from questions about outbreak transparency to the debate over defining ultra-processed foods.

and

, the challenges of tracing complex supply chains, and how whole genome sequencing and patient interviews help connect cases.

public notification of an E. coli outbreak linked to chicken wraps
, differing case counts in an
oyster-associated Salmonella outbreak
, and other recall updates.

USDA reorganization
and the
ongoing debate over how to define and regulate ultra-processed foods
.

news_title: Researchers assess antimicrobial resistance in Salmonella
efet_title: Researchers assess antimicrobial resistance in Salmonella
efet_body:
Scientists have identified certain antimicrobial resistance traits likely to spread through China’s food chain over the next 25 years.
Research by King’s College London and the Chinese Center for Disease Control and Prevention (China CDC) analyzed genetic traits linked to antimicrobial resistance in drug-resistant Salmonella across China’s food chain.
China is one of the largest producers and consumers of meat, so understanding how Salmonella and its resistance genes move through the chain could have implications for global food safety, said scientists.

news_title: Trader Joe's wraps named as source of ongoing E. coli outbreak - USA Today
efet_title: Trader Joe's wraps named as source of ongoing E. coli outbreak - USA Today
efet_body:
FOOD
Food Safety
Add Topic
Trader Joe's wraps named as source of ongoing E. coli outbreak
Mary Walrath-Holdridge
USA TODAY
Oct. 23, 2026
Updated Oct. 24, 2026, 12:45 p.m. ET
Hear this story
The source of an ongoing E. coli outbreak that has sickened at least 50 people was chicken wraps sold at Trader Joe's, federal health authorities confirmed.
The Department of Agriculture's Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS) confirmed the link in an email to USA TODAY on Friday, Oct. 23, following a
USA TODAY story about a lawsuit and investigation related to the outbreak.
The lawsuit, along with state investigation documents reviewed by USA TODAY, named Trader Joe's Tarragon Chicken Salad Wraps as the source.
Trader Joe's confirmed in an Oct. 20 email to USA TODAY that it pulled its Tarragon Chicken Salad Wraps from shelves in 9 states after the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) notified the chain in September that there may be a "possible issue" with them.
"The
E. coli
O157:H7 outbreak (2026-04) investigation identified ready-to-eat, multi-ingredient chicken wraps from certain Trader Joe’s stores as a common exposure among people who became sick," FSIS said in its statement. "The wraps reported by some cases very early in the investigation were proactively removed from the market by Trader Joe’s before a link to the outbreak was established."
The Food and Drug Administration, along with the USDA, had previously identified the source of the outbreak only as an unnamed "Ready-To-Eat Multi-ingredient wrap with chicken." The public
FDA
and
FSIS
entries for the outbreak still listed the unspecified wraps as of Friday, Oct. 23.
The USDA is still working alongside other agencies to investigate the ingredient that was the source, it said, and "extensive product testing" has all been negative. It is unlikely to be chicken, it added, as chicken is rarely the source of the outbreak strain of E. coli (E. coli O157:H7), also known as Shiga toxin-producing E. coli, or STEC, a type of foodborne illness that sometimes causes a serious condition that can lead to kidney damage called hemolytic uremic syndrome.
Historically, health agencies like the FDA and USDA have named multi-ingredient products during associated outbreaks, even if a specific ingredient within wasn't yet identified as the culprit. In this case, FSIS said the products were removed from shelves before a link could be confirmed and a recall could be initiated.
"FSIS quickly issues information to the public through recall releases and public health alerts when a product is linked to illnesses and there is actionable information for consumers. If an ongoing public health risk is identified, the agencies will take appropriate action," the statement read.
Food attorney Bill Marler, who is representing two women who say they became ill after eating the wraps in a lawsuit against Trader Joe's, told USA TODAY that he believes the FDA and USDA should have named the source publicly, even if products were pulled from shelves.
"The only thing that FSIS is hanging its hat on is that the product's off the shelf; there's no reason to tell anybody anything," he said. "But when they can identify the product or the processor or the grower, they should be open and tell the public. The public has the right to know."
